title: Mastering Claude (Anthropic)
subtitle: From first prompt to Projects, Artifacts, research, connectors and team rollout: work with Claude like an expert
description:
Claude is one of the most capable AI assistants available, but most people use a fraction of what it can do. This course takes you from solid chat fundamentals to expert workflows: choosing between a more capable and a faster model tier, analysing long documents, PDFs, images and charts, organising work in **Projects**, building interactive **Artifacts**, personalising Claude with styles and instructions, using research and extended thinking wisely, and running repeatable writing and editing workflows.

You will also get a clear, non-technical introduction to Claude Code, connectors and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and the Claude API, with optional *going further* sections for technical readers. The final module covers safety, privacy, data controls and how to roll Claude out responsibly across a team or agency. Every lesson includes copy-paste prompt templates, worked examples and a hands-on activity.
outcomes: Choose an appropriate Claude model tier and feature for a given task, balancing quality, speed and cost
Write structured prompts that give Claude context, a clear task, constraints and an output format
Analyse long documents, PDFs, images and charts with Claude and verify the results
Set up Projects with project knowledge and instructions for repeatable client or team work
Create, iterate on and share Artifacts such as documents, checklists and simple interactive tools
Explain Claude Code, connectors/MCP and the Claude API well enough to scope work with technical colleagues
Apply privacy, data-control and team usage policies when using Claude with business information

modules.summary: Understand how Claude works, how to choose between capable and fast model tiers, and the prompt structure experts use every day.

lessons.title: How Claude works and choosing the right model tier
lessons.body:
### What Claude actually is

Claude is a family of large language models built by Anthropic, available through the Claude apps (web, desktop and mobile), through the Claude API for developers, and through several cloud platforms. Under the hood, Claude predicts useful text one piece at a time based on everything in its **context**: your messages, any files you attach, instructions you set, and the conversation so far. It does not "look things up" in a hidden database unless a tool such as web search or a connector is switched on, and it does not remember other chats unless a memory or project feature explicitly provides that context.

Keeping this mental model in mind explains most of Claude's behaviour:

- **Better context in, better answer out.** Claude only knows what is in its training and what you put in front of it.
- **It can be confidently wrong.** Fluent text is not the same as verified fact, especially for recent events, niche figures and exact numbers.
- **It follows instructions closely.** Precise, explicit requests beat vague ones almost every time.

### The model family: capable vs fast

Anthropic releases Claude as a *family* of models rather than a single one. Names and version numbers change over time, so rather than memorising them, learn the pattern that has stayed stable:

- **The most capable tier** is best for complex reasoning, long multi-step tasks, nuanced writing, strategy, difficult analysis and agentic work (where Claude takes many steps on its own). It is typically slower and costs more per use on the API, and paid app plans may apply tighter usage limits to it.
- **A balanced tier** gives strong quality at higher speed and lower cost. For many everyday tasks (drafting, summarising, reformatting, brainstorming) it is the sensible default.
- **A fast, lower-cost tier** is built for speed and volume: classifying hundreds of comments, extracting fields from forms, quick rewrites, or powering high-traffic features in an app.

In the Claude apps you usually choose a model from a menu near the message box. Which models appear depends on your plan and may change; check Anthropic's official help centre or model overview page for the current line-up rather than relying on a blog post from last year.

### A simple decision rule

Ask two questions before you pick:

1. **How costly is a mediocre answer?** A board presentation, a legal-adjacent summary or a pricing strategy deserves the most capable tier. A first-draft caption does not.
2. **How many times will this run?** One-off thinking work favours capability; repeated, high-volume work favours speed and cost.

| Task | Sensible starting tier |
|---|---|
| Rewrite 200 product titles to a template | Fast tier |
| Draft a weekly client update from notes | Balanced tier |
| Analyse a 90-page contract for risks to discuss with a lawyer | Most capable tier |
| Plan a 6-month content strategy with trade-offs | Most capable tier |
| Tag 1,000 survey comments by sentiment (via API) | Fast tier, spot-checked |

If a cheaper tier produces weak results, do not immediately conclude "AI can't do this". First improve the prompt; then move up a tier and compare.

### Worked example: same task, two tiers

A creator in Dubai asks for a sponsorship pitch to a regional skincare brand. On a fast tier, the result is a clean but generic email. On the most capable tier, with the same prompt plus the brand's recent campaign notes, Claude connects the creator's audience data to the brand's launch, flags that the sponsored content must be clearly disclosed under local advertising rules, and proposes two package options. The lesson: capability matters most when the task requires *connecting* several pieces of context.

### Tokens and context windows in plain English

Claude reads and writes in **tokens**, which are small chunks of text (roughly parts of words). The **context window** is how much Claude can consider at once: your instructions, files and the conversation. Claude's context windows are large enough for long reports, books and big spreadsheets, but they are still finite. Very long chats can also degrade focus. When a conversation gets long and messy, start a fresh chat with a clean summary.

### Pitfalls

- Using the most capable tier for everything and hitting usage limits by lunchtime.
- Using the fastest tier for high-stakes analysis and trusting it without review.
- Assuming Claude knows today's news without web search.
- Treating model names from old tutorials as current.

### Privacy note

Whatever tier you choose, the same rule applies: do not paste information you are not permitted to share (client secrets, personal data of customers, passwords). Module 6 covers data controls in detail.
keyTakeaways: Claude only works with what is in its context: training, your messages, files, instructions and enabled tools.
Pick the most capable tier for complex, high-stakes reasoning; a balanced or fast tier for everyday and high-volume work.
If results are weak, improve the prompt first, then compare tiers.
Model names and availability change; check the official model overview and help centre.

knowledgeCheck.question: An agency needs to tag 5,000 short social comments by sentiment every week. Which starting choice is most sensible?
options: The most capable tier for every comment
Whichever tier appears first in the menu
No AI; tagging cannot be automated
A fast, lower-cost tier with human spot-checks
knowledgeCheck.explanation: High-volume, simple classification suits a fast tier; spot-checking catches errors. The most capable tier would be slower and costlier without clear benefit.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why might Claude give an outdated answer about a news event from last week?
options: Recent events are blocked by all AI providers
Without web search or supplied sources, Claude relies on training data that has a cut-off
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Models are trained up to a cut-off. Enable search (where available) or paste sources for anything recent.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the best first step when a cheaper model gives weak results on a task?
options: Give up on AI for that task
Repeat the same prompt ten times
Improve the prompt with context, constraints and an example, then compare tiers
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Prompt quality is often the bottleneck. Improve it, then test a more capable tier if needed.

lessons.activity: Pick one real task you do weekly. Run it on two different Claude model tiers with the same prompt and note differences in quality, speed and usefulness in a short table.

lessons.title: Chat fundamentals: the prompt structure experts use
lessons.body:
### Why structure beats cleverness

There are no magic words. Expert Claude users get better results because they give Claude what a smart new colleague would need: **context, a clear task, constraints and a format**. Claude is particularly responsive to clear, direct instructions and to well-organised input.

### The C-T-C-F framework

1. **Context:** who you are, who the audience is, what is going on, and why it matters.
2. **Task:** exactly what you want, using a verb ("draft", "compare", "critique", "extract").
3. **Constraints:** length, tone, must-include and must-avoid items, regional rules.
4. **Format:** bullets, table, email, JSON, headings; plus an example if you have one.

### Copy-paste template

```text
Context: I am a [role] at [company/type]. My audience is [who]. Background: [2-4 sentences].
Task: [Verb] a [deliverable] that [goal].
Constraints:
- Length: [x words / x bullets]
- Tone: [e.g. warm, confident, no hype]
- Must include: [points]
- Avoid: [jargon, claims we can't prove, emojis]
Format: [structure]. Here is an example of the style I like: [paste example]
Before you start, ask me up to 3 questions if anything important is missing.
```

That last line is powerful: it invites Claude to close gaps instead of guessing.

### Use XML-style tags to separate material

Claude handles clearly labelled sections well. When you paste several things (a brief, a transcript, a style guide), wrap each in simple tags so nothing gets mixed up:

```text
<brief>
Launch email for our Ramadan collection, UK and UAE audiences.
</brief>
<brand_voice>
Warm, respectful, understated. No discount language in the subject line.
</brand_voice>
<product_notes>
[paste notes]
</product_notes>
Using the brief, voice and notes above, write 3 subject lines and one email body under 150 words.
```

The tag names are yours to choose; consistency matters more than the exact words.

### Iterate like an editor, not a gambler

Your first response is a draft. Instead of regenerating randomly, give targeted feedback:

- "Keep the structure, but make paragraph two half as long."
- "The tone is too salesy for B2B finance buyers. Make it calmer and more specific."
- "Replace the generic benefits with the three customer quotes in my notes."

You can also **edit your earlier message** and resend it when you realise the original prompt was missing something; that often works better than piling on corrections.

### Worked example

A sales rep in Riyadh writes: "Write a follow-up email." Claude produces something polite but empty. Rewritten with C-T-C-F:

```text
Context: I sell B2B payroll software. I met Sara, HR Director at a 300-person logistics firm, at a conference on Tuesday. She mentioned manual overtime calculations cause month-end delays.
Task: Draft a follow-up email that proposes a 20-minute call.
Constraints: Under 120 words. Professional, not pushy. Mention the overtime pain point. No attachments or pricing.
Format: Subject line + email body.
```

The result references the specific pain, proposes two time slots and reads like a human wrote it. The difference came entirely from context.

### Ask for reasoning, critique and options

- "Give me three options with different angles, then recommend one and explain why."
- "Before answering, list the assumptions you are making."
- "Critique this draft as a sceptical CFO would. Be specific."

These prompts turn Claude from a text generator into a thinking partner.

### Pitfalls

- **Overlong prompts with no hierarchy.** Put the most important instruction clearly; use headings or tags.
- **Negative-only instructions.** "Don't be boring" helps less than "use one concrete example per paragraph".
- **Contradictions** such as "be detailed" and "keep it to 50 words".
- **Not saying who it is for.** Audience changes everything.

### Safety note

Structured prompts often include real details. Use placeholders (e.g. "[Client A]") when sharing sensitive names is not necessary for the task, and follow your organisation's AI policy.
keyTakeaways: Use Context, Task, Constraints and Format (C-T-C-F) for important prompts.
Wrap pasted materials in labelled tags so Claude can tell them apart.
Iterate with specific editorial feedback or edit the original prompt instead of regenerating blindly.
Invite Claude to ask clarifying questions before it starts.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which prompt is most likely to get a strong result?
options: Context: I run a bakery blog for home bakers. Task: Draft a 600-word post on using AI to plan weekly baking. Constraints: friendly tone, no hype. Format: H3 headings plus a checklist.
Write something good about AI for my blog, make it viral.
Write a blog post about AI.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Only the bakery prompt gives context, a clear task, constraints and a format.

knowledgeCheck.question: You paste a brief, a transcript and a style guide into one message. What helps Claude keep them separate?
options: Wrapping each in clearly labelled tags such as <brief> and <transcript>
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Labelled sections make it clear which material is which and reduce mix-ups.

knowledgeCheck.question: Claude's draft is 80% right but too long. What is the most efficient next step?
options: Start a new chat with no context
Give targeted feedback: keep the structure, cut to 150 words, remove paragraph 3
Regenerate until a shorter one appears
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Specific editorial feedback keeps what works and fixes what doesn't.

lessons.activity: Take a prompt you used recently and rewrite it using C-T-C-F plus tags. Run both versions and compare the outputs side by side.

lessons.title: Your first power session: a guided tour of the Claude workspace
lessons.body:
### The workspace at a glance

Whether you use Claude on the web, the desktop app or mobile, the core workspace is similar. Exact labels and menu positions change as the product evolves, and some features depend on your plan and region, so treat this as a map rather than a pixel-perfect screenshot.

- **The message box:** where you type, attach files and images, and choose options.
- **Model selector:** lets you switch between available model tiers.
- **Tools and feature toggles:** depending on your plan, options such as web search, research, extended thinking, and connected apps may appear here.
- **Chat history (sidebar):** your past conversations, which you can rename, star or delete.
- **Projects:** workspaces that group chats with shared knowledge and instructions (Module 3).
- **Settings:** profile, preferences, styles, privacy and data controls, connected tools.

### A 20-minute power session

Follow these steps with a real piece of your own work that contains no confidential data.

**Step 1: Set your profile preferences.** In settings, look for a place to tell Claude about yourself and how you like responses (for example, "I'm a marketing manager in Lahore; I prefer concise answers with bullet points and British spelling"). This is applied across chats where supported.

**Step 2: Start a focused chat.** One chat per task keeps context clean. Name it something searchable, like "Q4 newsletter draft".

**Step 3: Attach material.** Upload a document or paste text. Ask for a structured summary first:

```text
Summarise the attached document for a busy manager:
1. Purpose in one sentence
2. Five key points
3. Decisions or actions required
4. Anything unclear or missing
```

**Step 4: Turn the summary into a deliverable.** Ask Claude to produce a one-page brief or email based on the summary. If the output is a substantial standalone piece, Claude may place it in an Artifact panel you can edit, copy or download (Module 3).

**Step 5: Critique and improve.** Ask: "What would a sceptical reader challenge in this draft?" Then: "Revise to address the top two issues."

**Step 6: Save the pattern.** If this was useful, copy the prompts into a personal prompt library (a simple document works) or turn them into Project instructions.

### What a good first output looks like

When you run the summary prompt from Step 3 on, say, a 12-page supplier proposal, a strong response has a one-sentence purpose ("Proposal to supply packaging for the spring range at a fixed unit price for 12 months"), five specific key points with numbers where the document has them, a short list of decisions ("approve pricing tier", "confirm delivery schedule"), and a gaps section that says things like "No penalty terms for late delivery are stated". If your output is vaguer than that, add more context about who you are and what decision you face, then rerun.

### Keyboard and workflow habits

- Use **Shift+Enter** for new lines in the desktop and web message box so you can write structured prompts without sending early.
- **Edit and resend** your earlier message instead of adding "actually, I meant..." five times.
- **Branch deliberately:** if a conversation drifts, start a new chat and paste a short summary of the decisions so far.
- **Copy responses cleanly** using the copy button to preserve formatting.

### What to expect on different plans

Free access generally lets you try core chat features with usage limits. Paid individual plans typically add higher limits, more models and more features. Team and Enterprise plans add administration, shared projects and stronger data controls. Availability varies by plan and region and changes over time, so check Anthropic's official pricing and help centre pages for specifics rather than relying on this course for plan details.

### Pitfalls

- Mixing five unrelated tasks in one endless chat.
- Uploading sensitive client files to a personal account.
- Forgetting that responses can contain errors; always read before you send.

### Going further

If you work across many chats on the same client, jump ahead to Projects in Module 3. If you are technical, Module 5 explains how the same models are reached through the API and Claude Code.

video.script: Welcome to your first Claude power session. In the next few minutes, we will turn Claude from a chat box into a genuine work tool. Start with your profile preferences. Tell Claude who you are, what you do, and how you like answers: short or detailed, bullets or prose, British or American spelling. You only do this once, and every conversation starts closer to what you need. Next, open a new chat for one task only. Give it a clear name, like 'Q4 newsletter draft'. One task per chat keeps Claude focused. Now attach a document. Do not ask for a vague summary. Ask for structure: the purpose in one sentence, five key points, the decisions required, and anything unclear or missing. That last part is where Claude often catches gaps you missed. Then turn that summary into something useful: a one-page brief, an email to your manager, or a checklist. When the output is substantial, Claude may open it in a separate panel called an Artifact, which you can edit, copy or download. Here is the expert habit most people skip: ask Claude to critique its own work. 'What would a sceptical reader challenge here?' Then ask it to fix the top two issues. Finally, save what worked. Copy your best prompts into a simple prompt library. Next time, you start from a proven template instead of a blank box. Remember: features vary by plan and region, and Claude can make mistakes. You are the editor. Claude is the very fast first draft.

keyTakeaways: The workspace combines a message box, model selector, feature toggles, history, Projects and settings.
One chat per task keeps context clean; start fresh with a summary when a chat drifts.
Set profile preferences once so every chat starts closer to your style.
Plan and region determine available features; always check official help pages.

knowledgeCheck.question: Your chat about a campaign has drifted across three unrelated topics and answers are getting muddled. Best move?
options: Start a new chat and paste a short summary of the key decisions
Keep going; Claude will sort it out
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A fresh chat with a clean summary restores focus and removes irrelevant context.

knowledgeCheck.question: Where should you record how you generally like Claude to respond (for example, British spelling and concise bullets)?
options: In the file name of uploads
In profile or personal preference settings, where supported
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Profile preferences apply across chats, saving repetition.

lessons.activity: Complete the 20-minute power session with a non-confidential document from your work and save the three most useful prompts in a personal prompt library.

lessons.title: Long documents and file analysis
lessons.body:
### Why Claude is strong with long material

Claude supports large context windows, which means it can read long reports, contracts, research papers, transcripts and exported spreadsheets in a single conversation. That makes it excellent for questions like "What changed between these two policy versions?" or "Which clauses in this agreement affect payment timing?" The skill is not uploading; it is asking the right questions and verifying the answers.

### Supported inputs (conceptually)

In the Claude apps you can typically upload common document types such as PDFs, Word documents, plain text, CSV files and images, or paste text directly. File size and count limits vary by plan and change over time, so check the official help centre. For PDFs, Claude can generally consider both the text and the visual layout, including charts and tables, though scanned or low-quality pages may be read less reliably.

### The long-document workflow

**1. Orient first.** Before asking detailed questions, get a map:

```text
I've attached [document type]. Before we go deeper:
1. Describe its structure (sections and what each covers).
2. Identify the 5 most important points for a [role, e.g. marketing director].
3. List any sections that seem incomplete, contradictory or ambiguous.
```

**2. Ask targeted questions with quotes.** Ask Claude to ground answers in the text:

```text
Using only the attached document, answer: [question].
Quote the exact passages that support your answer and name the section or page.
If the document does not answer the question, say "Not stated in the document".
```

Requiring quotes has two benefits: it improves accuracy, and it lets you verify in seconds.

**3. Extract into structure.** Turn prose into tables:

```text
Extract every deliverable, deadline and responsible party from the attached statement of work.
Return a table with columns: Deliverable | Deadline | Owner | Section reference.
Mark anything ambiguous with "(check)".
```

**4. Compare documents.** Upload two versions and ask:

```text
Compare <v1> and <v2>. List every material change in a table:
Clause | Old wording (short) | New wording (short) | Practical impact for us.
Ignore formatting-only changes.
```

**5. Decide and draft.** Only after verification, ask Claude to draft the email, summary or negotiation points.

### Worked example

A small agency in Manchester receives a 40-page influencer-marketing agreement from a brand. They upload it and ask for obligations on the agency, payment terms, content approval rights, usage rights duration and exclusivity. Claude returns a table with section references, and flags that the usage rights clause allows perpetual paid-ads usage of creator content, which conflicts with the creators' standard 12-month licence. The account manager checks the quoted clause, confirms it, and asks Claude to draft a polite redline request. A lawyer still reviews the final contract, but the team walked in prepared rather than surprised.

### Tips for spreadsheets and CSVs

- Tell Claude what each column means if headers are cryptic.
- Ask for the method before the answer: "Explain how you will calculate churn, then do it."
- Where available, Claude can run analysis code to compute results; still spot-check a few rows yourself.
- For large datasets, ask for summary statistics and anomalies first, then drill down.

### Pitfalls

- **Assuming completeness.** Ask "What might you have missed?" and check sections that matter most.
- **Accepting unquoted claims** on contracts, compliance or finances.
- **Uploading more than needed.** If only chapter 3 matters, share chapter 3.
- **Scanned documents.** Poor scans can produce misreadings; verify numbers and names.
- **Legal or financial reliance.** Claude helps you prepare; qualified professionals make the call.

### Privacy note

Contracts, HR files and customer lists often contain personal or confidential data. Use an account type your organisation has approved, remove unnecessary personal details, and check data retention settings (Module 6).
keyTakeaways: Orient first: ask for structure, key points and gaps before detailed questions.
Require quotes and section references so every answer can be verified quickly.
Convert prose into tables for deliverables, deadlines, changes and risks.
Share only what is needed and use approved accounts for confidential files.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the main benefit of asking Claude to quote supporting passages from a document?
options: It lets you verify claims quickly and reduces unsupported answers
It is required for the upload to work
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Quotes ground the answer in the source and make verification fast.

knowledgeCheck.question: You need every deadline from a 30-page statement of work. Which prompt is best?
options: Extract every deliverable, deadline and owner into a table with section references; mark ambiguous items
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A structured extraction with references produces a checkable, usable output.

knowledgeCheck.question: A scanned PDF gives some odd numbers in Claude's summary. What should you do?
options: Check the numbers against the original pages, as low-quality scans can be misread
Trust the numbers; AI can't misread
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Scan quality affects accuracy; verify key figures against the source.

lessons.activity: Upload a long, non-confidential document (for example, a public annual report). Use the orient, quote, extract workflow and record one thing Claude found that you would have missed.

lessons.title: Vision: images, screenshots, charts and visual PDFs
lessons.body:
### What Claude's vision can do

All current Claude models accept images as input. In practice this means you can share a photo, screenshot, chart, slide, whiteboard, receipt, form or design mock-up and ask questions about it. Claude cannot generate images itself in the chat; it analyses them and can produce text, tables, code or diagrams-as-code in response.

High-value uses for professionals:

- **Charts and dashboards:** "What are the three most important trends in this analytics screenshot?"
- **Slides and ads:** "Critique this carousel for clarity, hierarchy and accessibility."
- **Handwritten notes and whiteboards:** "Transcribe and organise into action items."
- **Forms and receipts:** "Extract vendor, date, amount and tax into a table."
- **UI screenshots:** "Write step-by-step instructions for a new user based on this screen."
- **Competitor creative:** "Describe the visual strategy and messaging of these five ads."

### A reliable vision prompt

```text
I'm sharing [type of image]. Context: [what it is and why it matters].
1. Describe what you see, including any text, numbers and labels.
2. Answer: [specific question].
3. Tell me what you're uncertain about (small text, cropped areas, ambiguous colours).
```

Step 1 matters: asking Claude to describe first exposes misreadings before they flow into conclusions.

### Worked example: chart critique

A social media manager shares a screenshot of monthly engagement for a Pakistani fashion brand's account. Prompt: "Describe the chart, then give three insights and two questions I should ask the analytics team." Claude reads the axis labels, notes a sharp drop in one month, points out that the axis does not start at zero (which visually exaggerates change), and asks whether a posting-frequency change or a platform algorithm change coincided with the dip. The manager verifies the numbers in the native analytics tool before reporting.

### Tips for better results

- **Crop to what matters.** A focused image beats a full-screen capture with ten panels.
- **Use sufficient resolution** so small text is legible.
- **Label multiple images:** "Image 1 is the old landing page; Image 2 is the new one."
- **Ask for structured outputs:** tables, JSON or checklists make extraction easier to verify.
- **Combine with text:** paste the underlying numbers when you have them; vision is best for layout, context and quick reads.

### Sample output: receipt extraction

Suppose you upload three restaurant receipts from a client dinner and ask for a table with vendor, date, currency, subtotal, tax and total. A good response returns one row per receipt, notes the currency symbol it saw on each (for example AED or GBP), and adds a line such as "Receipt 2: the tax amount is partially obscured by a fold; please confirm". That uncertainty note is exactly what you want: it tells you which single number to check by eye instead of rechecking everything.

### Accessibility and design reviews

Claude can help check visual content for accessibility issues such as low contrast, text too small for mobile, missing alt text or reliance on colour alone. Ask: "Review this graphic for accessibility and suggest alt text under 125 characters." Treat its feedback as a helpful review, not a formal accessibility audit.

### Limits to respect

- Claude may misread tiny, blurred or rotated text, and can miscount many similar objects.
- Precise spatial measurement (exact pixel positions, exact angles) is not a strength.
- Do not use Claude to identify real people from their faces; Claude is designed not to do facial identification, and doing so raises serious privacy issues.
- For PDFs, visual elements are considered, but always verify numbers taken from charts.

### Privacy note

Screenshots often capture more than you intend: open tabs, customer names, email addresses, account numbers. Crop or blur before uploading. This is one of the most common accidental data leaks in AI use.

### Going further

Via the API, images and PDFs can be sent as part of a message, enabling workflows such as automatically extracting fields from invoices. Teams building this should add validation rules (for example, totals must equal line items) and human review for exceptions.
keyTakeaways: Claude analyses images, screenshots, charts and visual PDFs; it does not generate images in chat.
Ask Claude to describe what it sees first, then answer, then flag uncertainty.
Crop, label and use legible resolution; paste raw numbers when you have them.
Blur or crop personal data before uploading screenshots; do not use Claude to identify people from faces.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why ask Claude to describe an image before answering your question?
options: It surfaces misreadings early so they don't flow into conclusions
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A description step lets you spot misread labels or numbers before relying on the analysis.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which is an inappropriate use of Claude's vision capability?
options: Critiquing an ad for visual hierarchy
Identifying an unknown person from a photo of their face
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Facial identification of real people is not supported and raises serious privacy concerns.

knowledgeCheck.question: Before uploading a dashboard screenshot, what should you check?
options: That it is in black and white
That the screenshot is as large as possible
That no customer names, emails or other sensitive data are visible
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Screenshots often expose extra data; crop or blur before sharing.

lessons.activity: Take a screenshot of a chart or ad you work with (cropped of sensitive data). Use the three-step vision prompt and write down one insight and one misreading you caught.

lessons.title: Research and web search, with verification built in
lessons.body:
### Knowledge vs search vs research

Claude has broad knowledge from training, but that knowledge has a cut-off and can contain errors. Depending on your plan and region, Claude can also use **web search** to fetch current information and show sources, and a more thorough **research** mode that runs multiple searches and compiles a longer, cited report. Some plans also let Claude search connected workplace tools. Names and availability of these options change, so check the official help centre for what your plan includes.

Use each mode deliberately:

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Explain a concept, brainstorm, draft | Claude's own knowledge |
| Current facts, prices, news, recent regulations | Web search |
| Multi-angle investigation, market scan, literature review | Research mode, where available |
| Your company's own documents | Uploads, Projects or connectors |

### A research prompt that produces usable output

```text
Research question: [precise question].
Scope: [region, time period, industry]. Audience: [who will read this].
Please:
1. Search for current, authoritative sources (official sites, regulators, reputable publications).
2. Summarise findings with a citation for every factual claim.
3. Separate "well-established" from "contested or uncertain".
4. List what you could not find or verify.
Output: executive summary (5 bullets), then detail by sub-topic, then a source list.
```

### Worked example: disclosure rules for creators

An agency serving creators in the UK, UAE and US asks: "What are the current advertising disclosure requirements for paid influencer posts in the UK, UAE and US?" With web search on, Claude summarises guidance and cites official or reputable sources such as the UK advertising regulator, the US Federal Trade Commission and UAE media regulation sources, and notes that UAE rules include licensing considerations for influencers. The agency then opens each cited source to confirm the details and date, because regulations change and summaries can compress nuance.

### The verification habit (non-negotiable)

AI search reduces effort; it does not remove responsibility. For anything you will publish, advise on or spend money on:

1. **Open the cited source.** Does it actually say what the summary claims?
2. **Check the date.** Is it current for your purpose?
3. **Check authority.** Official regulator or primary source beats a random blog.
4. **Triangulate important facts** with at least one independent source.
5. **Watch for missing citations** on specific numbers; ask "Which source supports this figure?"

If Claude cannot cite a specific claim, treat it as unverified.

### Research without web access

If search is unavailable on your plan, you can still research well: paste or upload the sources yourself and ask Claude to synthesise only from them, citing which document each point comes from. This is often *more* reliable for professional work because you control the source set.

### Prompt-injection awareness

Web pages can contain hidden or misleading text designed to manipulate AI tools. Claude is trained to resist such instructions, but you should still be cautious when a search result seems to push Claude towards an odd conclusion, a particular product, or an action you did not ask for. Treat web content as data, not as instructions.

### Pitfalls

- Citing an AI summary instead of the underlying source.
- Asking broad questions ("Tell me about marketing") and getting broad answers.
- Using research mode for simple questions; it takes longer and uses more of your allowance.
- Forgetting regional differences in rules and prices.

### Going further

Through the API, developers can enable server-side web search and web fetch tools, and use citations features that point to exact passages in supplied documents. These make it easier to build research assistants with traceable answers.
keyTakeaways: Use Claude's knowledge for concepts, web search for current facts, research mode for multi-source investigations, where available.
Ask for citations on every factual claim and a list of what could not be verified.
Always open, date-check and triangulate important sources before publishing or advising.
Treat web content as data, not instructions; be alert to manipulation.

lessons.title: Projects and project knowledge
lessons.body:
### What a Project is

A **Project** in Claude is a workspace that groups related chats and gives them shared context. Typically a Project has:

- **Project knowledge:** documents, notes and reference files that Claude can draw on in every chat inside the Project.
- **Project instructions:** standing guidance (tone, audience, rules, output formats) applied to every chat in that Project.
- **Chats:** individual conversations that all start with that shared context.

On team plans, Projects can usually be shared with colleagues so everyone works from the same knowledge and instructions. Availability, sharing options and knowledge size limits vary by plan; check the official help centre.

### When to create a Project

Create one when you will return to the same context repeatedly:

- A **client account** (brand guidelines, product sheets, past campaigns, approval rules)
- A **recurring deliverable** (weekly newsletter, monthly performance report)
- A **course or research topic** (readings, notes, glossary)
- A **sales territory** (ideal customer profile, case studies, objection handling)

One-off questions do not need a Project.

### Designing great project knowledge

Quality beats quantity. Upload material that is current, authoritative and relevant:

1. **Brand voice guide** with do/don't examples.
2. **Product or service facts:** features, pricing policy statements, FAQs (kept up to date).
3. **Audience profiles:** who you serve and what they care about.
4. **Gold-standard examples:** two or three outputs you consider excellent.
5. **Rules and compliance:** disclosure requirements, claims you must not make, regional notes.

Remove outdated versions. If two documents conflict, Claude may blend them. Name files clearly, like "BrandVoice_2026.pdf", not "final_v3_REAL.pdf".

### Writing project instructions

```text
You are supporting the content team at [Agency] working for [Client], a [industry] brand serving [markets].
Always:
- Follow the brand voice guide in project knowledge.
- Use British spelling and a warm, confident tone.
- Include #ad or "Paid partnership" wording for any sponsored post.
- Flag any claim that needs substantiation (health, finance, "best", "No.1").
Never:
- Invent statistics, testimonials or prices.
- Mention competitors by name.
Default output: a draft, then 3 bullet notes on assumptions and risks.
If a request conflicts with project knowledge, ask before proceeding.
```

Keep instructions focused on durable rules. Put task-specific details in the chat itself.

### Worked example: a client Project

A boutique agency in Abu Dhabi creates a Project for a hospitality client. Knowledge: brand book, room and amenity fact sheet, three approved Instagram captions, and a list of phrases the legal team rejected. Instructions: tone, bilingual English/Arabic caption format, and disclosure rules. Now any team member can open a new chat and write "Draft 5 captions for the new rooftop brunch, family-friendly angle" and get on-brand drafts in seconds, with the rejected phrases avoided. When the fact sheet changes, one person updates the knowledge file and everyone benefits.

### Sample output: what "good" looks like

With the hospitality Project above, a request for five captions should return drafts that use the approved amenity names exactly as written in the fact sheet, include Arabic versions in the agreed format, avoid every rejected phrase, and end with a short note such as "Assumption: brunch price not included because it isn't in project knowledge". If drafts ignore the brand voice, your instructions are probably too long or too vague; shorten them and add one gold-standard example.

### Maintenance routine

- **Monthly:** remove outdated files, update facts, add new gold-standard examples.
- **After mistakes:** if Claude repeats an error, add a clear rule or example to the instructions.
- **Access review:** on shared Projects, check who has access, especially after staff or client changes.

### Pitfalls

- Dumping every file you own into knowledge, which dilutes relevance.
- Contradictory instructions across the Project and your profile preferences.
- Storing confidential data in a Project shared more widely than intended.
- Forgetting that knowledge is only as accurate as the files you uploaded.

### Going further

Conceptually, Projects give Claude a curated context package. Developers build similar behaviour through the API with system prompts plus retrieved documents; the design principles (curate, label, keep current) are the same.
keyTakeaways: Projects combine shared knowledge, standing instructions and chats for recurring work.
Curate knowledge: current, authoritative, relevant, clearly named, no conflicting versions.
Put durable rules in project instructions and task details in the chat.
Review shared Projects regularly for accuracy and access.

lessons.title: Artifacts: create, iterate and share
lessons.body:
### What Artifacts are

**Artifacts** are standalone pieces of content Claude creates in a dedicated panel beside the chat, rather than inline in the conversation. They are designed for things you will reuse, edit or share, such as:

- Documents (briefs, reports, policies, scripts) in formatted text
- Checklists, tables and templates
- Code snippets and simple web pages
- Diagrams expressed as code (for example, flowcharts)
- Small interactive tools such as calculators, quizzes or planners

Claude usually decides when to create an Artifact, based on whether the content is substantial and self-contained, but you can ask explicitly: "Create this as an artifact." Sharing and publishing options depend on your plan and settings; on team plans, admins may control whether Artifacts can be shared. Check the help centre for current options.

### Why they matter for non-engineers

Artifacts let you build useful mini-tools without writing code yourself. You describe what you want in plain language; Claude writes the code and shows a working preview. For example:

```text
Create an interactive artifact: an influencer campaign budget calculator.
Inputs: number of creators, average fee per creator, content usage fee (%), agency margin (%).
Outputs: total creator cost, usage cost, agency fee, total client price.
Style: clean, mobile-friendly, labels in plain English. Show example numbers pre-filled.
```

Claude produces a working calculator you can test immediately. Then you iterate:

- "Add a currency selector for GBP, USD, AED, SAR and PKR (labels only, no conversion)."
- "Add a reset button and make the total bold."
- "Add a note that figures are estimates and exclude tax."

### Iterating well

Artifacts support versioning within the conversation, so you can refer back to earlier versions. Good iteration habits:

1. **Change one thing at a time** for complex artifacts.
2. **Describe the bug precisely:** "When I enter 0 creators, the total shows NaN. Show 0 instead."
3. **Ask for a summary of what changed** after each revision.
4. **Keep a clean copy** of versions you approve.

### Document artifacts for teams

For written work, ask for artifacts with structure:

```text
Create an artifact: a one-page creative brief for [campaign].
Sections: Objective, Audience, Key message, Mandatories (including disclosure), Deliverables, Timeline, Approvals.
Use short bullets. Leave [TBC] where information is missing rather than inventing it.
```

The "[TBC] instead of inventing" instruction is a small habit that prevents plausible-sounding fabrication.

### Worked example

A sales team lead in Karachi needs a discovery-call checklist. She asks Claude for an artifact with 12 questions grouped into Situation, Pain, Impact and Next Steps, plus checkboxes and a notes field. Within minutes she has an interactive checklist, tweaks the wording to fit her market, and shares it with her team to use in calls.

### Pitfalls

- **Treating an artifact tool as production software.** A calculator built in minutes is great for internal use; anything handling payments, personal data or client-facing logic needs proper review and testing.
- **Hidden errors in formulas.** Test with known numbers and edge cases (zeros, very large values).
- **Sharing publicly by accident.** Check what a share link exposes before sending it.
- **Embedding real personal data** in an artifact that might be shared.

### Sample prompt: a content calendar artifact

```text
Create an artifact: a 4-week content calendar table for a coffee shop's Instagram.
Columns: Week | Day | Format (Reel/Carousel/Story) | Topic | Caption hook | Call to action | Status.
Three posts per week. Leave Status as "Draft". Don't invent promotions or prices.
```

Good output is a tidy table you can copy into a spreadsheet, with varied formats, hooks that match the brief, and no made-up offers. You can then ask: "Add a column for the local holiday or event each week, marking [TBC] where unsure."

### Safety note

Artifacts that run code do so in a sandboxed preview. Still, do not paste secrets like API keys or passwords into artifacts, and do not ask them to collect personal information from others without a lawful basis and proper tools.
keyTakeaways: Artifacts are standalone, editable outputs such as documents, checklists, code and small interactive tools.
Non-engineers can build internal mini-tools by describing them in plain language and iterating.
Iterate one change at a time, describe bugs precisely and test with edge cases.
Check sharing settings and never embed secrets or unnecessary personal data.

lessons.title: Styles, custom instructions and memory
lessons.body:
### Three layers of personalisation

Claude offers several ways to shape responses without repeating yourself. Exact names and availability vary by plan and change over time, but the layers are:

1. **Profile or personal preferences:** account-wide information about you and how you like answers.
2. **Styles:** reusable writing styles you can select for a response, such as more concise, more explanatory, or a custom style built from samples of your own writing.
3. **Project instructions:** rules that apply only inside a specific Project (previous lesson).

Some plans also offer **memory** features that let Claude reference past conversations or remember details you've shared, with controls to view, edit or turn memory off. Where memory exists, you should know how to check and manage it.

### Setting preferences well

Good preferences are short, stable and general:

```text
About me: I'm a freelance social media strategist working with beauty and wellness brands in the UK and Gulf region.
How I like responses:
- Lead with the answer, then detail.
- Use British spelling.
- Bullets over long paragraphs for plans; prose for client-facing copy.
- When you're unsure, say so rather than guessing.
- Don't add emojis unless I ask.
```

Avoid putting task-specific or confidential information here; it applies everywhere.

### Building a custom style from your writing

Styles are most useful for people who write a lot in a consistent voice (creators, marketers, founders). To create a custom style, you typically provide samples of your writing or describe the style. Tips:

- Use 3 to 5 samples that represent your best, most typical writing.
- Include variety (a post, an email, a longer article) so the style generalises.
- Describe what matters: sentence length, humour, formality, words you never use.
- Test the style on a new topic and refine.

A creator from Lahore who writes witty, bilingual English/Urdu-transliterated captions can build a style from her best posts, then ask for drafts that already sound like her, cutting editing time dramatically.

### Choosing the right layer

| Need | Best layer |
|---|---|
| "I always want British spelling" | Profile preferences |
| "Write this one in my newsletter voice" | Custom style |
| "For Client X, always include disclosure wording" | Project instructions |
| "For this post only, make it playful" | The chat message |

### Sample test for a new style

After creating a style, test it on a topic you have never written about, such as "a short post announcing our new opening hours". Compare it with a real post you wrote. Check sentence length, openings, humour and sign-offs. If the draft overuses one quirk (for example, every sentence starts with a question), add a line to the style description such as "Use rhetorical questions at most once per post", and test again. Two or three rounds of refinement usually produce a style you can rely on for first drafts.

### Managing memory responsibly

Where memory is available:

- **Review what is remembered** periodically in settings.
- **Delete or correct** outdated or sensitive items.
- **Use incognito or temporary chats** (where offered) for sensitive or one-off topics you do not want remembered.
- **Separate work and personal use**; do not mix client work into a personal account.

### Pitfalls

- Conflicting instructions between layers (profile says "be brief", project says "be comprehensive"). Be explicit about which wins for a task.
- Over-personalising so every output sounds identical; sometimes you need a different voice.
- Assuming a custom style guarantees accuracy. Style affects voice, not facts.

### Privacy note

Anything you put in preferences, styles or memory may influence many future responses. Keep it free of passwords, financial details, health information or client secrets.
keyTakeaways: Personalise at the right layer: profile, style, project instructions or the chat itself.
Keep profile preferences short, stable and non-confidential.
Build custom styles from 3 to 5 representative writing samples and test them.
Where memory exists, review, correct and delete it, and use temporary chats for sensitive topics.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Account-wide preferences are the right layer for rules that apply everywhere.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Client-specific rules belong in that client's Project.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which is a good practice for AI memory features where available?
options: Periodically review, correct or delete remembered items and use temporary chats for sensitive topics
Never look at what is stored
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Actively managing memory keeps it accurate and protects sensitive information.

modules.title: Deeper thinking and writing workflows
modules.summary: Use extended thinking for hard problems and run professional writing workflows that keep your voice and your facts intact.

lessons.title: Extended thinking: when deeper reasoning pays off
lessons.body:
### What extended thinking is

Claude can spend more effort reasoning before it answers. In the apps this is usually presented as an option to turn on extended or deeper thinking for a response; on the API, developers can enable thinking and control how much effort Claude spends. Recent models can also decide adaptively how much to think based on the task. When thinking is on, Claude works through the problem step by step before producing its final answer, and the app may show a summary of that reasoning.

The trade-off is simple: **more thinking usually means better answers on hard problems, but slower responses and more usage.** For easy tasks it adds delay without adding value.

### When to turn it on

Turn on deeper thinking for tasks with many interacting parts or where mistakes are costly:

- Multi-step maths, pricing models and forecasts
- Strategy with trade-offs ("Which of these three markets should we enter first and why?")
- Complex analysis across several documents
- Debugging logic, formulas or code
- Planning projects with dependencies and constraints
- Evaluating arguments and finding flaws

Leave it off for:

- Quick rewrites, translations and summaries
- Brainstorming lists
- Formatting and extraction with a clear template

### Prompts that make thinking count

Thinking works best when the problem is well defined:

```text
Problem: [describe clearly].
Constraints: [budget, time, resources, rules].
Options to consider: [A, B, C] (add others if they are clearly better).
Evaluate each option against: [criteria with weights if you have them].
Then recommend one, state your key assumptions, and say what new information would change your recommendation.
```

The last sentence is valuable: it tells you which facts to check before acting.

### Worked example: pricing a retainer

A two-person agency in Jeddah wants to price a social media retainer. They share their hours per deliverable, freelancer costs, target margin and three competitor price ranges they collected themselves. With deeper thinking on, Claude builds the cost per month, tests three pricing tiers, identifies that the lowest tier barely covers costs if revisions exceed two rounds, and recommends capping revisions in the contract. Without thinking, the answer was quicker but missed the revision risk. The agency still checks the arithmetic in a spreadsheet before sending the proposal.

### Sample output shape

With the template above, a strong thinking-assisted answer usually follows a clear shape: a restatement of the problem and constraints, a short comparison table scoring each option against your criteria, a recommendation in one or two sentences, a list of three to five assumptions, and a closing "what would change my mind" section (for example, "If average revisions per deliverable exceed three, the mid tier becomes unprofitable"). If you don't get that shape, ask for it explicitly.

### Reading the reasoning

When a reasoning summary is shown, skim it for:

- **Wrong assumptions** ("assuming 20 working days" when you work 22)
- **Misread inputs** (a number or constraint taken incorrectly)
- **Skipped options** you care about

Correct the assumption and ask Claude to rerun. The reasoning is a helpful window, not a guarantee that the final answer is correct.

### Thinking vs better prompts vs bigger model

These are three separate levers:

| Lever | Helps when |
|---|---|
| Better prompt | The task is unclear or missing context (most common problem) |
| More capable model tier | The task needs more knowledge, nuance or skill |
| Deeper thinking | The task needs careful multi-step reasoning |

Often the best results combine all three for hard, high-stakes problems.

### Pitfalls

- Turning thinking on for everything and wondering why you hit usage limits.
- Believing longer reasoning means certainty; verify numbers independently.
- Giving an underspecified problem and expecting thinking to fill in the missing facts.

### Going further

On the API, thinking can be combined with tool use so Claude reasons between steps (for example, searching, then reasoning about results, then searching again). Developers can tune effort to balance quality, latency and cost; check the official documentation for current parameters.
keyTakeaways: Extended thinking trades speed and usage for better answers on complex, multi-step problems.
Use it for strategy, maths, multi-document analysis and debugging; skip it for simple rewrites.
Well-defined problems with constraints and criteria get the most from thinking.
Check shown reasoning for wrong assumptions and still verify key numbers.

options: Comparing three market-entry options against weighted criteria and constraints
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Multi-criteria strategic trade-offs need careful multi-step reasoning.

knowledgeCheck.question: Claude's reasoning summary shows it assumed 20 working days per month, but you work 22. What should you do?
options: Correct the assumption and ask Claude to rerun the analysis
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Reasoning summaries help you catch and fix wrong assumptions.

options: Improve the prompt with the missing context
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Thinking cannot supply facts you didn't provide; fix the prompt first.

lessons.title: Writing and editing workflows that sound like you
lessons.body:
### Claude as writing partner, not ghostwriter

Claude is widely regarded as a strong writer and editor. The most effective professionals do not ask it to "write something" and publish the result. They use it at each stage of a writing workflow: planning, drafting, critiquing, editing and adapting.

### The five-stage workflow

**1. Plan.** Clarify the goal before any drafting.

```text
I need to write [piece] for [audience] to achieve [goal].
Ask me 5 questions that would most improve this piece. Then propose 2 outline options with different angles.
```

**2. Draft from your raw material.** Supply notes, voice memos transcribed, bullet points, or examples. Claude writes better when it shapes your ideas than when it invents its own.

```text
Turn my notes below into a [format] draft. Keep my examples and opinions; don't add new claims.
Voice: [describe or select a style].
<notes>
[paste]
</notes>
```

**3. Critique.** Ask Claude to review as a specific reader.

```text
Review this draft as [a sceptical procurement manager / a busy founder / a first-time customer].
List the 5 biggest weaknesses in order of impact, with a suggested fix for each. Don't rewrite yet.
```

**4. Edit precisely.** Use targeted edit requests:

- "Tighten by 30% without losing the three examples."
- "Rewrite the opening to lead with the customer problem."
- "Replace abstract claims with concrete details from my notes."
- "Check for passive voice and jargon; list them, then fix."

**5. Adapt.** Repurpose one piece into many:

```text
From the approved article below, create:
1. A LinkedIn post (under 200 words, one insight, one question at the end)
2. Three X/Twitter posts
3. A newsletter intro (80 words)
4. A 45-second video script with a hook in the first line
Keep facts identical. Add #ad disclosure only if I mark the content as sponsored.
```

### Editing someone else's work

For managers and editors, Claude can give consistent feedback at scale:

```text
Edit the draft below for clarity and grammar only. Do not change meaning or voice.
Return: (1) the edited version, (2) a list of every change with a short reason.
```

Asking for a change list keeps you in control and helps writers learn.

### Worked example: founder newsletter

A skincare founder in London records a rambling 10-minute voice note about why she reformulated a product. Claude turns the transcript into a 500-word newsletter using her own phrases, flags two claims ("clinically proven", "best on the market") as needing substantiation under advertising rules, and suggests softer, accurate alternatives. She edits one paragraph and sends. The piece sounds like her because it is made from her words.

### Sample critique output

When you run the critique prompt on a sales one-pager as "a sceptical procurement manager", good feedback is specific and ranked: "1. No price anchor or range, so I can't assess budget fit. Fix: add a starting-from figure or pricing model. 2. The claim 'saves hours every week' has no example. Fix: add one customer scenario with before/after steps. 3. Implementation effort isn't mentioned..." If the feedback is generic ("make it more engaging"), ask Claude to cite the exact sentence each point refers to.

### Avoiding "AI voice"

Generic AI prose tends to overuse certain patterns: grand openings, lists of three adjectives, predictable transitions, and empty conclusions. Counter it by:

- Supplying your own examples, stories and opinions
- Specifying banned phrases
- Asking for "plain, specific language; one idea per paragraph"
- Reading the draft aloud before you publish

### Ethics and disclosure

Be honest about AI assistance where your organisation, client, publication or platform requires it. Academic institutions and some publishers have specific policies. Never present AI-generated testimonials, reviews or quotes as real.

### Pitfalls

- Publishing without a human read-through.
- Letting Claude introduce facts you didn't provide.
- Losing your voice by accepting every suggestion.
keyTakeaways: Use Claude across the workflow: plan, draft from your material, critique, edit and adapt.
Drafts built from your notes and examples sound like you and contain fewer invented claims.
Ask for critique from a specific reader's perspective before rewriting.
Request change lists when editing to keep humans in control; never fabricate testimonials.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which approach produces the most authentic founder newsletter?
options: Ask Claude to write about the brand from scratch
Give Claude the founder's own notes or transcript and ask it to shape them without adding new claims
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Drafting from the founder's own material preserves voice and accuracy.

knowledgeCheck.question: You want feedback before a rewrite. Which prompt fits?
options: Review as a sceptical procurement manager; list the five biggest weaknesses with fixes; don't rewrite yet
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A specific reader lens and a no-rewrite instruction produce actionable critique.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why ask for a list of changes when Claude edits a colleague's draft?
options: So you can review each change and the writer can learn from it
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A change log keeps edits transparent and reviewable.

lessons.activity: Take one piece you need to write this week and run it through all five stages. Keep the critique list and note which suggestions you rejected and why.

lessons.title: Coding help and Claude Code, explained for non-engineers
lessons.body:
### You don't need to be a developer to benefit

Claude is highly capable at writing, explaining and fixing code. For non-engineers, that opens doors: spreadsheet formulas, small automations, website tweaks, data cleanup scripts, and understanding what your developers are talking about. You do not need to become a programmer, but you do need to know what to ask and how to check the result.

### Everyday coding help in chat

Useful non-engineer requests:

- **Spreadsheet formulas:** "Write a Google Sheets formula that returns the campaign with the highest ROAS from columns A (name) and D (ROAS). Explain how it works."
- **Explaining code:** "Explain this tracking snippet line by line in plain English. What data does it send, and where?"
- **Small scripts:** "Write a script that renames all images in a folder to lowercase with hyphens. Explain how to run it safely on a copy first."
- **Website edits:** "Here is my landing page HTML. Add a FAQ section with these five questions, matching the existing style."

A safe prompt pattern:

```text
I'm not a developer. I want to [goal] using [tool: Google Sheets / Excel / WordPress / Python].
Please:
1. Give me the solution.
2. Explain what each part does in plain English.
3. Tell me how to test it safely (on a copy or sample).
4. List what could go wrong and how I'd notice.
```

### What Claude Code is

**Claude Code** is Anthropic's agentic coding tool. Instead of chatting about code, developers give Claude Code a task and it works directly with a codebase: reading files, making changes across many files, running commands and tests, and iterating until the task is done, with the developer approving actions according to permission settings. It is available in the terminal and through integrations such as IDE extensions, desktop and web experiences; exact surfaces and plan availability change, so check the official documentation.

For a non-engineer, a useful analogy: chat is like asking an expert for advice over the phone; Claude Code is like giving a skilled contractor supervised access to the workshop to do the job, while you approve the important steps.

### Why it matters to marketers, founders and managers

- **Faster delivery:** developers can move faster on routine changes such as landing pages, integrations, bug fixes and tests.
- **Better scoping:** you can ask your team whether a task is "a Claude Code job" (well-defined, testable) or needs deeper design work.
- **Prototypes:** founders and product managers increasingly prototype ideas with agentic coding tools, then hand them to engineers for hardening.

### Governance questions to ask your team

1. Which repositories and environments can the tool access?
2. What actions require human approval (running commands, pushing code, touching production)?
3. How are secrets such as API keys kept out of prompts and logs?
4. Is all AI-written code reviewed and tested before release?

### Going further (for technical readers)

Claude Code works best with:

- **A project guidance file** describing conventions, commands and architecture, so Claude follows your team's standards.
- **Clear, testable tasks:** "Add input validation to the signup form and write tests" beats "improve the signup".
- **Plan first:** ask it to propose a plan before editing, review the plan, then let it execute.
- **Tight feedback loops:** tests, linters and type checks let Claude verify its own work.
- **Least privilege:** restrict permissions and review diffs before merging.

It can also connect to external tools through MCP (next lesson), such as issue trackers or documentation sources.

### Pitfalls

- Running a script you don't understand on real data. Always test on a copy.
- Pasting code that contains passwords or API keys into any AI tool.
- Assuming working code is secure code; security review still matters.
- Letting an agent act on production systems without approvals.
keyTakeaways: Non-engineers can use Claude for formulas, small scripts, explanations and website edits, always testing on copies.
Claude Code is an agentic coding tool that works directly in a codebase with human-approved actions.
Ask governance questions about access, approvals, secrets and code review before adopting agentic tools.
Technical users get best results with guidance files, testable tasks, plan-first and least privilege.

lessons.title: Connectors and the Model Context Protocol (MCP)
lessons.body:
### The problem connectors solve

By default, Claude only knows what is in its training and what you paste or upload. But your real work lives in other tools: email, calendars, documents, CRMs, project trackers, design tools, analytics. **Connectors** let Claude access information and, in some cases, take actions in those tools, with your permission.

### What MCP is

The **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** is an open standard introduced by Anthropic for connecting AI applications to external tools and data sources. Think of it like a universal adapter: instead of every AI app building a custom integration for every tool, a tool can offer an MCP server once, and any MCP-compatible AI application can connect to it.

Key concepts in plain English:

- **MCP server:** a connector that exposes a tool's capabilities, for example "search documents", "create a task" or "read calendar events".
- **MCP client:** the AI application (such as the Claude apps or Claude Code) that connects to servers.
- **Tools:** actions the AI can call (search, create, update).
- **Resources:** data the AI can read (files, records).

Because MCP is an open standard, it is supported across a growing ecosystem, including by other AI vendors and developer tools.

### Connectors in the Claude apps

Depending on your plan, Claude offers a directory of connectors for popular services, and on some plans you can add custom connectors that point to remote MCP servers. Organisation admins on team plans typically control which connectors are allowed. Availability varies by plan and region; check the help centre.

### Practical workflows

With appropriate connectors enabled, you can ask things like:

```text
Look through my calendar for next week and my recent emails with [client].
Prepare a one-page briefing for Tuesday's meeting: open issues, commitments we made, and questions to ask.
Cite which email or event each point comes from.
```

```text
Search our shared drive for the latest brand guidelines and the Q3 campaign report.
Summarise what worked, what didn't, and three recommendations for Q4.
```

```text
From this meeting summary, create tasks in our project tracker for each action item, assigned as listed. Show me the list before creating anything.
```

Notice the last line: **ask to review before actions are taken.** Reading is low-risk; writing, sending or deleting deserves confirmation.

### Security and trust

Connectors are powerful, so treat them with care:

- **Least privilege:** only connect tools you need, with the narrowest permissions.
- **Trust the source:** use official or vetted connectors; a malicious MCP server could expose data or misbehave.
- **Prompt injection:** content inside documents, emails or web pages can contain instructions aimed at AI. Claude is trained to resist these, but you should still review actions, especially ones that send data out.
- **Approve actions:** keep confirmation steps for sending, deleting or sharing.
- **Audit:** on team plans, admins should review which connectors are enabled and who uses them.

### Worked example

A sales manager connects Claude to her CRM and email (as approved by IT). Before a quarterly review she asks Claude to list deals that have not had contact in 30 days, summarise the last interaction for each, and draft a personalised check-in for review. She edits and sends the drafts herself. The work that took an afternoon now takes 30 minutes, and nothing was sent without her approval.

### Going further (for technical readers)

MCP servers can run locally or remotely. Developers can build servers with official SDKs in several languages, and the Claude API offers an MCP connector feature that lets Messages API requests connect to remote MCP servers. Design good tools with clear names and descriptions, validate inputs, and log actions.
keyTakeaways: Connectors give Claude permissioned access to your tools; MCP is the open standard behind many of them.
MCP servers expose tools and resources; AI apps such as Claude act as MCP clients.
Reading is low-risk; require review before Claude sends, creates or deletes anything.
Use least privilege, vetted connectors and admin oversight to manage security and prompt-injection risk.

lessons.title: The Claude API for teams: core concepts without code
lessons.body:
### Why managers and marketers should understand the API

The Claude apps are for people chatting with Claude. The **Claude API** is for software talking to Claude: your website chatbot, an internal tool that drafts proposals, an automation that classifies support tickets. Even if you never write code, understanding the building blocks lets you scope projects, estimate costs conceptually and ask good questions of developers or vendors.

### The building blocks

**1. Messages.** Every request sends a list of messages: turns from the "user" (your application) and, in multi-turn conversations, previous "assistant" replies. The API is stateless: the application sends the relevant conversation history each time. Claude replies with a new assistant message.

**2. System prompt.** A special instruction that sets Claude's role, rules and context for the whole interaction, like project instructions for software. For example: "You are a support assistant for [Brand]. Answer only from the provided help articles. If unsure, offer to connect the customer with a human."

**3. Model choice.** The application specifies which model to use. The same tier logic from Module 1 applies: fast tiers for high-volume simple tasks, capable tiers for complex reasoning.

**4. Tokens and cost.** Usage is billed by input and output tokens, with different prices per model. Features such as prompt caching (reusing a long, repeated prefix) and batch processing (asynchronous bulk requests) can reduce cost for suitable workloads. Always check the official pricing page for current figures.

**5. Tool use.** Developers can describe tools, such as "look up order status" or "check stock", with a name, description and input format. Claude decides when a tool is needed and returns a structured request; the application runs the tool and sends the result back; Claude then continues. Anthropic also offers server-side tools such as web search, and features for structured outputs, citations, file handling and vision.

**6. Stop reasons and limits.** Responses indicate why Claude stopped (finished, hit the length limit, or wants to use a tool). Applications handle each case.

### A concept map of a simple support assistant

```text
Customer question
  -> App sends: system prompt + help-article excerpts + conversation history + question
  -> Claude replies, or requests tool "get_order_status(order_id)"
  -> App runs tool, returns result to Claude
  -> Claude writes final answer, cites the help article
  -> App shows answer; escalates to a human if confidence is low or the topic is sensitive
```

### Questions to ask before building

1. **What is the job?** One clear task beats a vague "AI assistant".
2. **What data does it need, and are we allowed to send it?**
3. **Which model tier,** and what are the estimated volume and cost?
4. **How will we evaluate quality?** Build a test set of real examples with expected answers before launch.
5. **What are the guardrails?** Topics to refuse, when to hand off to humans, disclosure that users are talking to AI where required.
6. **How are keys secured?** API keys belong in secure server-side storage, never in browser code, spreadsheets, prompts or chat messages.

### Worked example

An e-commerce brand in the UK wants to auto-draft replies to common customer emails. The team defines five categories, writes a system prompt with tone rules and refund policy excerpts, uses a fast tier for classification and a more capable tier for drafting complex complaints, and keeps a human approval step. They test on 200 past emails, compare drafts with what agents actually sent, refine, then launch gradually.

### Security note

Never paste an API key into a chat, a shared document or a course exercise. If a key is exposed, revoke it immediately in the console and create a new one. Set spending limits and monitor usage.
keyTakeaways: The API connects software to Claude using messages, a system prompt and a chosen model.
Usage is billed by tokens; caching and batch processing can reduce cost for suitable workloads.
Tool use lets Claude request actions your application performs and returns results for.
Plan evaluation, guardrails, human hand-off and secure key storage before launch.
